```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.pos = "H", fig.align = "center", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4)

library(tidyverse)
library(glmnet)
library(boot)
library(gridExtra)
library(caret)

f2 <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) # rounds numbers for the text and tables, e.g. f2(13.8) gives "13.80"

permtestPCA <- function (X, nTests = 100, alpha = 0.05, center.data = TRUE, scale.data = TRUE, ...){ # permutation test function from lecture 5
  n <- nrow(X)
  m <- ncol(X)
  X <- scale(X, center = center.data, scale = scale.data)
  res.X      <- prcomp(X)
  eigs.X     <- res.X$sdev^2
  eigs.Xperm <- matrix(0, m, nTests)
  Xperm      <- matrix(0, n, m)
  Xperm[, 1] <- X[, 1]
  for (i in 1:nTests){
    for (j in 2:m) {
      ind <- sort(runif(n), index.return = TRUE)$ix   # random permutation of the rows
      Xperm[, j] <- X[ind, j]
    }
    eigs.Xperm[, i] <- prcomp(Xperm)$sdev^2
  }
  perc.alpha <- matrix(0, m, 2)
  for (s in 1:m){
    perc.alpha[s, ] <- quantile(eigs.Xperm[s, ], c(alpha/2, 1 - alpha/2))
  }
  plot(1:m, eigs.X, type = "b", col = "red", main = "Permutation test PCA",
       xlab = "Component", ylab = "Eigenvalue", ...)
  lines(1:m, perc.alpha[, 1], type = "b", col = "blue")
  lines(1:m, perc.alpha[, 2], type = "b", col = "blue")
  legend("topright", inset = .05, c("Observed", "2.5% bound", "97.5% bound"),
         lty = 1, col = c("red", "blue", "blue"), pch = "o")
  return(perc.alpha)
}

athletics  <- read.csv("data_783996yw.csv")  # 1000 institutions with revenue
prediction <- read.csv("predictions-2.csv")  # 10 institutions, revenue has to be predicted
```

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
# 1. Inspect data

dim(athletics) # check size, variables and distribution of revenue, the variable of interest
str(athletics)
summary(athletics$revenue)

na_counts <- colSums(is.na(athletics)) # check missing values for each variable/column
na_counts[na_counts > 0] # show only cols with missing values. hc na counts match with hc salary na counts

table(no_men_teams = athletics$teams_men == 0, hc_men_missing = is.na(athletics$hc_men)) # institution with no men's team can't have men's hc!
table(no_women_teams = athletics$teams_women == 0, hc_women_missing = is.na(athletics$hc_women)) # same for women
min(athletics$ac_men, na.rm = TRUE) # ac counts are never 0 (min = 1), so na in ac_men means no acs at the institution

sum(!is.na(athletics$ac_men)   & is.na(athletics$ac_salary_men)) # how many institutions have acs but no salary reported?
sum(!is.na(athletics$ac_women) & is.na(athletics$ac_salary_women)) # probably volunteers (eada leaves them out of the average salary)

table(athletics$classification) # get an overview of categorical variables and their levels
table(athletics$sector) # some classifications and sectors have very small levels:
                        # NCCAA Division I, Private for-profit 4-year or above, Private nonprofit 2-year

revenue <- ggplot(athletics, aes(revenue / 1e6)) +  # inspect the revenue variable, divide by one million for easier reading
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "blue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Revenue of athletics programs", x = "Revenue (in million USD)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
revenue # a very skewed histogram...log it to combat skewness

logrevenue <- ggplot(athletics, aes(log(revenue))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "purple", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Log revenue", x = "log(revenue)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
logrevenue # roughly symmetric

grid.arrange(revenue, logrevenue, ncol = 2) # both histograms next to each other

# 2. Clean up the data

count_vars  <- c("ugrad_men", "ugrad_women", "athletes_men", "athletes_women", "teams_men", "teams_women", # the predictors are grouped by variable type
                 grep("^partic_", names(athletics), value = TRUE), # add all the partic_ variables more quickly
                 "hc_men", "hc_women", "ac_men", "ac_women") # logged
salary_vars <- c("hc_salary_men", "hc_salary_women", "ac_salary_men", "ac_salary_women") # logged
share_vars  <- c("hc_fulltime_share", "hc_female_share") # 0 to 1, not logged
num_vars    <- c(count_vars, salary_vars, share_vars)   # all 28 numerical predictors

fixed_coaches <- function(x) {
  for (s in c("men", "women")) { # loop runs once for men's and once for women's variables (hc, ac, salaries)
    hc <- paste0("hc_", s); ac <- paste0("ac_", s) # becomes hc_men and ac_men, then hc_women and ac_women
    hs <- paste0("hc_salary_", s); as <- paste0("ac_salary_", s) # same for the salary columns
    no_hc <- is.na(x[[hc]])          # institutions without hcs
    no_ac <- is.na(x[[ac]])          # institutions without acs
    x[[hc]][no_hc] <- 0              # missing coaches become 0 (no men's team -> no men's hc)
    x[[ac]][no_ac] <- 0
    x[[hs]][no_hc & is.na(x[[hs]])] <- 0 # no coaches -> salary also becomes 0
    x[[as]][no_ac & is.na(x[[as]])] <- 0 # coaches present but no salary (volunteers?) stay na for now, imputed after the split
  }
  x
}

logged_vars <- function(x) { # skewed variables, we log them
  for (v in c(count_vars, salary_vars)) x[[v]] <- log1p(x[[v]]) # log(x + 1) in case x is 0
  x
}

athletics_new  <- athletics %>% fixed_coaches() # the function fixed_coaches is applied to both datasets
prediction_new <- prediction %>% fixed_coaches()

colSums(is.na(athletics_new[num_vars]))[colSums(is.na(athletics_new[num_vars])) > 0] # only some ac salaries are still missing (the potential volunteers)

athletics_new$log_revenue <- log(athletics_new$revenue) # this is the target variable

athletics_new$classification  <- factor(athletics_new$classification) # categorical variables transformed to factors, for both datasets
athletics_new$sector          <- factor(athletics_new$sector)
prediction_new$classification <- factor(prediction_new$classification, levels = levels(athletics_new$classification)) # same levels -> same dummies
prediction_new$sector         <- factor(prediction_new$sector, levels = levels(athletics_new$sector))
stopifnot(!anyNA(prediction_new$classification), !anyNA(prediction_new$sector)) # check: every level in prediction exists in the data

athletics_new  <- logged_vars(athletics_new) # log the skewed predictors in both datasets
prediction_new <- logged_vars(prediction_new)
```

```{r split, include=FALSE}
# 3. Split the data

set.seed(123)
trainRowNumbers <- createDataPartition(athletics_new$log_revenue, p = 0.8, list = FALSE) # step 1: row numbers for the training data (80%)
train_data <- athletics_new[trainRowNumbers, ]  # step 2: training dataset
test_data  <- athletics_new[-trainRowNumbers, ] # step 3: test dataset
table(train_data$classification) # are all levels in the training set?

train_medians <- sapply(train_data[num_vars], median, na.rm = TRUE) # medians from the training data only (no leakage)
impute <- function(x) { # remaining na (salaries of potential volunteers) -> training median
  for (v in num_vars) x[[v]][is.na(x[[v]])] <- train_medians[v]
  x
}
train_data     <- impute(train_data)
test_data      <- impute(test_data)
prediction_new <- impute(prediction_new)
stopifnot(!anyNA(train_data[num_vars]), !anyNA(test_data[num_vars]), !anyNA(prediction_new[num_vars])) # check if no na is left

cor_tab <- sort(sapply(train_data[num_vars], cor, y = train_data$log_revenue), decreasing = TRUE) # correlation with log revenue
round(cor_tab, 2) # salaries and coaches correlate strongly with log revenue (in eada revenue must cover expenses)
```

```{r pca, include=FALSE}
# 4. PCA on the 28 numerical predictors (training data)
# dummies are left out for now, they return in the pcr (pca on 0/1 variables is hard to interpret)

X_pca      <- train_data[, num_vars] # predictors of the training set
X_pca_test <- test_data[, num_vars]  # predictors of the test set
p          <- ncol(X_pca)            # 28 variables

fitpca <- princomp(X_pca, cor = TRUE, scores = TRUE) # pca on the correlation matrix (variables have different units)
summary(fitpca)                                      # sd, vaf and cumulative vaf per component
eigenvalues <- fitpca$sdev^2                         # variance of each component
vaf         <- eigenvalues / p                       # proportion vaf (eigenvalues of a correlation matrix sum to p)
cum_vaf     <- cumsum(vaf)

screeplot(fitpca, npcs = p, type = "lines", main = "Scree plot", las = 1) # elbow plot
abline(h = 1, col = "red", lty = 2)                                       # red line = kaiser
k_kaiser <- sum(eigenvalues > 1)      # kaiser: a pc has to explain more than one original variable
k_vaf80  <- which(cum_vaf >= 0.80)[1] # first pc where 80% of the variance is reached

set.seed(123) # conduct a permutation test
perm_range <- permtestPCA(X_pca, nTests = 1000) # plot and matrix with the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles per eigenvalue
round(cbind(Eigenvalue = eigenvalues, Lower = perm_range[, 1], Upper = perm_range[, 2])[1:8, ], 3)
k_perm <- which(eigenvalues <= perm_range[, 2])[1] - 1 # keep pcs up to the first one that is not above chance

my_boot_pca <- function(x, ind){ # run pca on the resampled rows and return the eigenvalues
  res <- princomp(x[ind, ], cor = TRUE)
  return(res$sdev^2)
}

set.seed(123) # run the bootstrap
fit.boot  <- boot(data = X_pca, statistic = my_boot_pca, R = 1000)
eigs.boot <- fit.boot$t # store the bootstrapped eigenvalues (1000 x 28 matrix)

kaiser_boot <- data.frame(PC = 1:p, Eigenvalue = eigenvalues, # is the eigenvalue sig. > 1? yes if the whole 95% confidence interval is above 1
                          Lower = apply(eigs.boot, 2, quantile, 0.025),
                          Upper = apply(eigs.boot, 2, quantile, 0.975))
kaiser_boot$Significant <- kaiser_boot$Lower > 1
round(kaiser_boot[1:8, 1:4], 3)
k_kaiser_boot <- which(!kaiser_boot$Significant)[1] - 1

par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 1) + 0.1) # boxplot of the bootstrapped eigenvalues, red line = kaiser
boxplot(eigs.boot[, 1:10], las = 1, xlab = "Dimension", ylab = "Eigenvalue", col = "beige",
        main = "Bootstrapped eigenvalues")
abline(h = 1, col = "red", lty = 2)

pc_selection <- data.frame( # overview of the methods
  Method = c("Kaiser (eigenvalue > 1)", "80% cumulative VAF", "Permutation test", "Bootstrapped Kaiser"),
  PCs = c(k_kaiser, k_vaf80, k_perm, k_kaiser_boot))
pc_selection

n_pc <- k_perm # chosen number of pcs (permutation test)

vaf.boot   <- rowSums(eigs.boot[, 1:n_pc, drop = FALSE]) / p # bootstrapped proportion of variance explained by the chosen n_pc components
perc.alpha <- quantile(vaf.boot, c(0.025, 1 - 0.025)) # 95% percentile interval
round(100 * c(VAF = cum_vaf[n_pc], perc.alpha), 1)
hist(vaf.boot, xlab = paste("Proportion of variance explained by", n_pc, "PCs"), las = 1, col = "blue",
     main = "Bootstrap Confidence Interval", breaks = 20, border = "white")
abline(v = perc.alpha, col = "green", lwd = 2) # green: 95% interval
abline(v = cum_vaf[n_pc], col = "red", lwd = 2) # red: estimate on the training data

print(fitpca$loadings[, 1:n_pc], digits = 2) # weights of the variables in each pc

corpca  <- cor(X_pca, fitpca$scores)[, 1:n_pc] # diagnostics: fit per variable = squared correlations between variables and scores
fit_var <- cbind(corpca, Fit = rowSums(corpca^2))
round(fit_var, 2)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) # in the biplots points = institutions, arrows = variables
biplot(fitpca, pc.biplot = TRUE, scale = 1, choices = 1:2, col = c("blue", "red"),
       asp = 1, cex = c(0.4, 0.7), xlabs = rep("o", nrow(X_pca)), main = "Biplot components 1 and 2")
biplot(fitpca, pc.biplot = TRUE, scale = 1, choices = 2:3, col = c("blue", "red"),
       asp = 1, cex = c(0.4, 0.7), xlabs = rep("o", nrow(X_pca)), main = "Biplot components 2 and 3")
par(op)
```

```{r pcr, include=FALSE}
# 5. Principal component regression: log revenue on the n_pc pc scores + classification and sector dummies
# the pcs summarise the 28 numerical predictors, the dummies add the categorical information

train_scores <- data.frame(fitpca$scores[, 1:n_pc, drop = FALSE], # pc scores of the training data
                           classification = train_data$classification,
                           sector = train_data$sector,
                           log_revenue = train_data$log_revenue)
test_scores  <- data.frame(predict(fitpca, newdata = X_pca_test)[, 1:n_pc, drop = FALSE], # test projected on the training pca
                           classification = test_data$classification,
                           sector = test_data$sector)
fit_pcr <- lm(log_revenue ~ ., data = train_scores) # ols on pcs and dummies (lm makes the dummies itself)
summary(fit_pcr)
```

```{r ridge, include=FALSE}
# 6. Ridge regression on the 28 numerical predictors + dummies

form_x <- as.formula(paste("~", paste(c(num_vars, "classification", "sector"), collapse = " + ")))
y      <- train_data$log_revenue                     # dependent variable
X      <- model.matrix(form_x, data = train_data)    # predictor variables as a matrix, with dummies
X      <- X[, -1]                                    # remove intercept column (is fitted by glmnet)
X_test <- model.matrix(form_x, data = test_data)[, -1]
X_new  <- model.matrix(form_x, data = prediction_new)[, -1]
stopifnot(ncol(X_new) == ncol(X), ncol(X_test) == ncol(X)) # check: same 50 columns in all three matrices

x_mean <- colMeans(X[, num_vars]) # numerical columns turned into z-scores, with the means and sds of the training data
x_sd   <- apply(X[, num_vars], 2, sd)
X[, num_vars]      <- scale(X[, num_vars],      center = x_mean, scale = x_sd)
X_test[, num_vars] <- scale(X_test[, num_vars], center = x_mean, scale = x_sd)
X_new[, num_vars]  <- scale(X_new[, num_vars],  center = x_mean, scale = x_sd)

grid <- 10^seq(-5, 2, length.out = 100) # grid of lambdas (wide enough that lambda.min is not at the edge)
result.ridge <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = grid, standardize = FALSE) # ridge regression (alpha = 0), already standardised
plot(result.ridge, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE, las = 1) # coefficients shrink towards 0 but never become exactly 0

set.seed(123) # 10-fold cross validation
result.ridge.cv <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = grid, nfolds = 10, standardize = FALSE)
print(result.ridge.cv$lambda.min) # best cross validated lambda
print(result.ridge.cv$lambda.1se) # 1se rule: largest lambda within one standard error of the minimum

result.ridge.cv$cvm  <- result.ridge.cv$cvm^0.5 # mse -> rmse, on the same scale as y
result.ridge.cv$cvup <- result.ridge.cv$cvup^0.5
result.ridge.cv$cvlo <- result.ridge.cv$cvlo^0.5
plot(result.ridge.cv, ylab = "Root Mean-Squared Error")

result.ridge.min <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = result.ridge.cv$lambda.min, standardize = FALSE) # final runs with lambda.min
result.ridge.1se <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0, lambda = result.ridge.cv$lambda.1se, standardize = FALSE) # and lambda.1se
Weights <- cbind(result.ridge.min$beta, result.ridge.1se$beta) # coefficients on log scale (per sd for the numerical predictors)
colnames(Weights) <- c("lambda.min", "lambda.1se")
round(Weights, digits = 3)
```

```{r evaluation, include=FALSE}
# 7. Evaluation on log scale and on revenue scale

rmse   <- function(y, yhat) sqrt(mean((y - yhat)^2))
y_test <- test_data$log_revenue

pred_log <- list( # test predictions of log revenue
  "PCR"              = as.numeric(predict(fit_pcr, newdata = test_scores)),
  "Ridge lambda.min" = as.numeric(predict(result.ridge.min, newx = X_test)),
  "Ridge lambda.1se" = as.numeric(predict(result.ridge.1se, newx = X_test)))
# exp(log prediction) transforms the predictions back to usd; it estimates the median revenue and underestimates the mean

rev_test <- test_data$revenue
eval_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pred_log), function(m) { # one row per model
  pl <- pred_log[[m]]
  data.frame(Model = m,
             RMSE_log = rmse(y_test, pl),                                  # error on log scale (~ relative error)
             R2_log   = 1 - sum((y_test - pl)^2) / sum((y_test - mean(y_test))^2),
             RMSE_rev_M = rmse(rev_test, exp(pl)) / 1e6)                    # error in million usd, after exp()
}))
print(eval_tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

err_by_class <- data.frame(classification = test_data$classification, # where do the dollar errors come from?
                           sq_err_log = (y_test - pred_log[["Ridge lambda.min"]])^2,
                           sq_err_rev = (rev_test - exp(pred_log[["Ridge lambda.min"]]))^2) %>%
  group_by(classification) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), RMSE_log = sqrt(mean(sq_err_log)), RMSE_rev_M = sqrt(mean(sq_err_rev)) / 1e6,
            share_of_squared_err = sum(sq_err_rev)) %>%
  mutate(share_of_squared_err = share_of_squared_err / sum(share_of_squared_err)) %>% # share of the total squared usd error
  arrange(desc(RMSE_rev_M))
print(err_by_class, n = Inf) # fbs schools cause most of the dollar error

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) # observed vs predicted log revenue, red line = perfect prediction
plot(pred_log[["PCR"]], y_test, pch = 20, col = "grey40", las = 1, main = "PCR",
     xlab = "Predicted log revenue", ylab = "Observed log revenue")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
plot(pred_log[["Ridge lambda.min"]], y_test, pch = 20, col = "grey40", las = 1, main = "Ridge (lambda.min)",
     xlab = "Predicted log revenue", ylab = "Observed log revenue")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
par(op)
```

```{r predictions, include=FALSE}
# 8. Predictions for the 10 institutions, with the same models that were evaluated on the test set

new_scores <- data.frame(predict(fitpca, newdata = prediction_new[, num_vars])[, 1:n_pc, drop = FALSE], # projected on the training pca
                         classification = prediction_new$classification, sector = prediction_new$sector)
pl_pcr   <- as.numeric(predict(fit_pcr, newdata = new_scores))     # log revenue predictions
pl_ridge <- as.numeric(predict(result.ridge.min, newx = X_new))    # X_new was standardised with the training means/sds

pred_out <- data.frame(id = prediction_new$id, classification = prediction_new$classification, # in million usd
                       rev_PCR_M   = exp(pl_pcr) / 1e6,     # back to usd with exp()
                       rev_Ridge_M = exp(pl_ridge) / 1e6)
print(pred_out, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pred_out, "predictions_output.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

# 1. Introduction

Intercollegiate athletic programs are an important part of higher education in the United States, and running such a program requires substantial financial resources. However, not every program generates the same amount of revenue. While some larger athletic programs may earn over \$100 million USD per year, many programs at smaller colleges have less than \$1 million USD available for their teams. For college athletic directors, it is therefore useful to know what revenue can be expected for a program with certain characteristics. This may aid them with planning their budget and comparing their program to similar institutions. Colleges and universities that participate in federal student aid programs have to report information about their athletic programs to the US Department of Education ([USDE](https://ope.ed.gov/athletics/#/)), for example about the number of college athletes, as well as the coaches and their respective salaries. Many of these characteristics are closely related, since larger programs usually have more athletes and more coaches at the same time. It is therefore relevant to investigate whether this information can be used to estimate the revenue of a program, and whether a few general features of a program already contain as much information as all characteristics together. Using the reported information from the USDE, the aim of this report is to answer two research questions. To begin with, **to what extent can the revenue of an intercollegiate athletic program be predicted from a few underlying program characteristics, compared with using all characteristics separately?** Secondly, based on this, **which characteristics, either on their own or combined into these underlying features, are most closely related to revenue?** Since this is a first exploratory analysis, the focus is on prediction and on relationships with revenue, without making claims about what causes differences in revenue.

# 2. Data

The data come from the Equity in Athletics Disclosure Act (EADA) survey of the US Department of Education. Every co-educational college or university that participates in federal student aid programs and has at least one intercollegiate athletic program annually reports information about its programs (USDE, 2026). The dataset used for this report contains 1,000 institutions. Two variables are categorical: the athletic association and division of the institution (19 levels, e.g. NCAA Division I-FBS) and its sector (5 levels, e.g. private nonprofit, 4-year or above). The other 28 variables, which are used as predictors, describe undergraduate enrollment, the number of athletes and teams, the participants per sport, the number and average salaries of head and assistant coaches, and the shares of full-time and female head coaches, mostly separately for men and women. The number of athletes counts each athlete once, while the participants per sport count an athlete once for every team they are on (USDE, 2026). The unit ID identifies the institution and is not used as a predictor. The variable of interest is the total revenue of the athletic program, which includes, for example, ticket sales, media rights, donations and support from the institution itself. Since revenue has to cover the expenses of the program, a deficit paid by the institution also counts as revenue (USDE, 2025). Revenue is very right-skewed: it ranges from \$13,766 to \$289.6 million, with a median of \$4.1 million and a mean of \$14.3 million (Appendix, Figure 1). Therefore, the logarithm of revenue, which is much more symmetric, is used as the dependent variable.

To evaluate the predictions on data that are not used for estimation, the 1,000 institutions are randomly split into a training set of 800 institutions (80%) and a test set of 200 institutions (20%). The split is stratified on log revenue, so that both sets contain small as well as large programs.

Missing values only occur in the coaching variables. Institutions without men's or women's teams report no coaches for those teams, so the number of coaches and their salaries are set to zero. For 10 institutions, assistant coaches are reported without a salary (16 missing salary values in total). As volunteer coaches are left out of the average salary (USDE, 2026), these may be programs with only volunteers. However, since this cannot be verified, the missing salaries are replaced by the median of the training data. The coach counts, the other counts and the salaries are also right-skewed, so they are transformed with $\log(1 + x)$, which keeps zeros defined and reduces the influence of very large programs.

A second dataset contains 10 institutions for which the revenue is predicted. Their unit IDs are replaced by the numbers 1 to 10.

# 3. Methods

The first technique is Principal Component Analysis (PCA). PCA tries to describe the variables in a dataset as well as possible by a few new, uncorrelated variables, called principal components. This is useful when variables are strongly correlated and therefore largely measure the same thing. Each component is a weighted sum of the original variables and can often be interpreted as a general feature of the observations, such as their size. PCA is unsupervised: it only uses the predictors, not the dependent variable.

Let $\mathbf{X}$ be the $n \times p$ matrix of predictors $X_1, \dots, X_p$, with $n$ observations and $p$ predictors. Component $s$ is the linear combination $Z_s = \gamma_{1s}X_1 + \dots + \gamma_{ps}X_p = \boldsymbol{\gamma}_s^\top \mathbf{X}$, where $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_s$ is the loading vector with the weights of component $s$. The first component has the largest possible variance:
$$
\max_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1:\, \|\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1\| = 1} \text{Var}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1^\top \mathbf{X}) = \max_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1:\, \|\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1\| = 1} \boldsymbol{\gamma}_1^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \boldsymbol{\gamma}_1,
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \text{Var}(\mathbf{X})$ is the covariance matrix, and the restriction $\|\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1\| = 1$ prevents an infinitely large variance. The solution is the first eigenvector of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and $\text{Var}(Z_1)$ is the first eigenvalue $\lambda_1$. Each next component again has maximum variance, but is uncorrelated with the previous ones, which gives $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots \geq \lambda_p$. Since PCA is sensitive to the scale of the variables, it is done on the correlation matrix, which is the same as using z-scores. The eigenvalues then add up to $p$, and the proportion of variance accounted for by component $s$ is $\text{VAF}_s = \lambda_s / p$.

To decide how many components $r$ to keep, four methods are used. First, the cumulative VAF should be at least 80%, although this can lead to many components. Second, Kaiser's rule keeps components with $\lambda_s > 1$, since a component equal to one standardised variable would have $\lambda_s = 1$. Third, in the scree plot of $\lambda_s$ against $s$, the components are retained up to the elbow, without the elbow itself. Fourth, the permutation test compares each $\lambda_s$ to the eigenvalues of $N_{\text{perm}} = 1000$ datasets in which the values within each column are randomly permuted, which removes the correlations between the predictors. If $\lambda_s$ lies above the $1 - \alpha/2$ percentile of the permuted eigenvalues, with $\alpha = 0.05$, dimension $s$ is significantly different from random data and is kept.

The stability of the eigenvalues and the VAF is assessed with the bootstrap. $B = 1000$ datasets $\mathbf{X}^{*b}$ of size $n \times p$ are drawn by sampling rows of $\mathbf{X}$ with replacement, and in each the eigenvalues $\lambda_s^{*b}$ are computed. Their 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles give a 95% confidence interval, where a narrow interval means a stable result. An eigenvalue is significantly larger than 1 (Kaiser's rule) if the whole interval lies above 1, and an interval is also constructed for the cumulative VAF of the selected components.

To interpret the components, the component loadings are used: the correlations between the variables and the component scores, $\rho_{js} = \text{cor}(X_j, Z_s) = \gamma_{js}\lambda_s^{1/2}$ for standardised variables. They lie between $-1$ and $+1$, and large positive or negative values show which variables a component represents, so that it can be named. A biplot shows the observations as points and the variables as arrows for the first two components. The fit per variable, $\sum_{s=1}^{r} \rho_{js}^2$, is the proportion of the variance of $X_j$ accounted for by the first $r$ components; a value close to 1 means the variable is well represented.

In the principal component regression (PCR), the dependent variable is regressed with Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) on the first $r$ component scores and dummy variables for the categorical predictors:
$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \sum_{s=1}^{r} \theta_s z_{is} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} \delta_l d_{il} + \varepsilon_i,
$$
where $y_i$ is the dependent variable for observation $i$, $\beta_0$ the intercept, $z_{is}$ the score on component $s$ with coefficient $\theta_s$, $d_{il}$ the $l$-th of $L$ dummies with coefficient $\delta_l$, and $\varepsilon_i$ the error term. For each component, the following hypotheses are tested:
$$
H_0: \theta_s = 0 \quad \text{versus} \quad H_1: \theta_s \neq 0.
$$
The null hypothesis $H_0$ states that component $s$ has no relation with the dependent variable, given the other components and the dummies, while the alternative hypothesis $H_1$ states that it does. The test uses the $t$-value $t = \hat{\theta}_s / \text{SE}(\hat{\theta}_s)$, which is the estimate divided by its standard error. The $p$-value is the probability of finding a $t$-value at least this large in absolute value if $H_0$ is true. If $p < 0.05$, which in large samples corresponds to $|t| > 1.96$, $H_0$ is rejected and the component is significant at the 5% level. A higher $R^2$ is preferred, as more variance of the dependent variable is then explained by the model.

The second technique is ridge regression, an adaptation of multiple regression that penalises the size of the coefficients. It is very useful with many or strongly correlated predictors, because the estimates become more stable. With the dependent variable in deviation from its mean, ridge regression minimises
$$
L(\beta_1, \dots, \beta_q) = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big( y_i - \sum_{j=1}^{q} x_{ij}\beta_j \Big)^2}_{\text{regression term}} + \underbrace{\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{q} \beta_j^2}_{\text{penalty term}},
$$
where $q$ is the number of predictors including dummies, $x_{ij}$ the value of predictor $j$ for observation $i$, $\beta_j$ its regression weight, and $\lambda > 0$ the penalty parameter (not the eigenvalues $\lambda_s$ of the PCA). Ridge regression shrinks the $\beta_j$ towards zero, and $\lambda$ controls the strength of this shrinkage: as $\lambda \to 0$ the estimates become the OLS estimates, and as $\lambda \to \infty$ they go to zero. The ridge estimates always exist, even under multicollinearity. Because all weights are penalised equally, the numerical predictors are standardised to z-scores. Ridge regression is preferred over the LASSO, as the LASSO can set coefficients to zero and tends to keep only one of several strongly correlated predictors, whereas ridge regression keeps all of them.

The value of $\lambda$ is chosen from a grid with $K$-fold cross-validation ($K = 10$): each fold $k$ is left out once, the model is estimated on the other folds, and the $n_k$ observations in fold $k$ are predicted, which gives
$$
\text{MSE}_k = \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{i \in \text{fold } k} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2, \qquad \text{RMSE}_{\text{CV}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \text{MSE}_k},
$$
where $\hat{y}_i$ is the out-of-sample prediction for observation $i$. A lower $\text{RMSE}_{\text{CV}}$ is better. Both $\lambda_{\min}$, with the lowest $\text{RMSE}_{\text{CV}}$, and $\lambda_{1SE}$, the largest $\lambda$ within one standard error of this minimum, are considered; the latter gives a simpler model with more shrinkage.

Both models are estimated on the training set and compared on the test set with $\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}$ and $R^2 = 1 - \sum_{i}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 / \sum_{i}(y_i - \bar{y})^2$, where $m$ is the number of test observations and $\bar{y}$ their mean. A lower RMSE and a higher $R^2$ mean better predictions. For a log-transformed dependent variable, errors on the log scale can be read as relative errors. Predictions are transformed back to the original scale with $\exp(\hat{y}_i)$, which estimates the median rather than the mean, since $E[\exp(y)] > \exp(E[y])$. On the original scale, the RMSE is mostly determined by the largest observations.

# 4. Results

```{r res-values, include=FALSE}
fbs      <- "classificationNCAA Division I-FBS"
pcr_sum  <- summary(fit_pcr)
share_fbs <- err_by_class$share_of_squared_err[err_by_class$classification == "NCAA Division I-FBS"]
n_fbs     <- err_by_class$n[err_by_class$classification == "NCAA Division I-FBS"]
share_d1  <- sum(err_by_class$share_of_squared_err[grepl("NCAA Division I", err_by_class$classification) &
                                                   !grepl("Division II", err_by_class$classification)])
```

The first principal component has an eigenvalue of `r f2(eigenvalues[1])` and explains `r f2(100 * vaf[1], 1)`% of the variance of the 28 predictors (Appendix, Table 1). The selection methods do not all agree with each other. The 80% VAF rule suggests `r k_vaf80` components, Kaiser's rule `r k_kaiser`, the bootstrapped Kaiser's rule `r k_kaiser_boot`, the scree criterion two (the eigenvalues drop sharply after the second component), and the permutation test `r k_perm`. Since the permutation test is the only method that compares the eigenvalues to those of random data, `r n_pc` components are selected. Components 4 to 6 have eigenvalues above 1, but not above what can be expected by chance. Together, the `r n_pc` components explain `r f2(100 * cum_vaf[n_pc], 1)`% of the variance, and the narrow bootstrap interval of [`r f2(100 * perc.alpha[1], 1)`%, `r f2(100 * perc.alpha[2], 1)`%] shows that this result is stable.

The loadings (Appendix, Table 2) and the biplot (Appendix, Figure 2) show what the components mean. The first component correlates positively with all variables, most strongly with the number of athletes, teams and coaches, so it measures *program size*. The second component is high for programs at large institutions with high coach salaries and many full-time coaches, and low for programs with many teams and coaches but lower salaries. It can be called *pay versus breadth*. The third component separates track and field and other individual sports from basketball, baseball and softball. Most variables are well represented by the three components, except the share of female head coaches and the number of football players.

In the PCR, the components and the dummies explain `r f2(100 * pcr_sum$r.squared, 1)`% of the variance of log revenue. Program size and pay versus breadth are significant at the 5% level ($t$ = `r f2(pcr_sum$coefficients["Comp.1", "t value"], 1)` and $t$ = `r f2(pcr_sum$coefficients["Comp.2", "t value"], 1)`, both $p < 0.001$), but the third component is not ($t$ = `r f2(pcr_sum$coefficients["Comp.3", "t value"], 2)`, $p$ = `r f2(pcr_sum$coefficients["Comp.3", "Pr(>|t|)"], 2)`). The division is also very important: an NCAA Division I-FBS program earns about `r round(exp(coef(fit_pcr)[fbs]))` times as much as a CCCAA program with the same component scores. For ridge regression, cross-validation chooses a very small penalty ($\lambda_{\min}$ = `r formatC(result.ridge.cv$lambda.min, format = "e", digits = 1)`), so the results are close to OLS. The largest ridge coefficients are again the division dummies, followed by the salary of head coaches of men's teams.

On the test set (Appendix, Table 3), both models predict log revenue well. The PCR has the lowest RMSE on the log scale (`r f2(eval_tab$RMSE_log[1], 3)`, $R^2$ = `r f2(eval_tab$R2_log[1], 3)`), so three components and the division contain almost the same information as all 28 characteristics. Since the errors are on the log scale, an RMSE of `r f2(eval_tab$RMSE_log[1], 3)` means that a predicted revenue is typically off by a factor of about $\exp(`r f2(eval_tab$RMSE_log[1], 2)`) \approx `r f2(exp(eval_tab$RMSE_log[1]), 1)`$. On the original scale, ridge regression with $\lambda_{\min}$ has the lowest RMSE (`r f2(eval_tab$RMSE_rev_M[2], 2)` million USD). These errors in USD mainly come from the largest programs: the `r n_fbs` FBS programs in the test set cause `r round(100 * share_fbs)`% of the squared error. The predicted revenues of the 10 new institutions (Appendix, Table 4) range from `r f2(min(pred_out$rev_PCR_M), 1)` million USD for the NAIA Division I program to `r f2(pred_out$rev_PCR_M[1], 1)` (PCR) and `r f2(pred_out$rev_Ridge_M[1], 1)` million USD (ridge) for the FBS program.

# 5. Conclusions and Discussion

The first research question was to what extent the revenue of an athletic program can be predicted from a few underlying characteristics, compared with using all characteristics separately. Revenue can be predicted quite well. A model with three components and the athletic division explains `r round(100 * eval_tab$R2_log[1])`% of the variance of log revenue in the test data, which is about the same as ridge regression with all 28 characteristics (`r round(100 * eval_tab$R2_log[2])`%). So a few general features of a program contain almost all the useful information. However, a prediction is still typically off by a factor of about `r f2(exp(eval_tab$RMSE_log[1]), 1)`, and the errors in USD are largest for the biggest programs. The models are therefore useful as a rough benchmark for athletic directors, but not for predicting the exact revenue of one program. The second research question was which characteristics are most closely related to revenue. Revenue is mainly related to the size of a program, and to a lesser extent to how well its coaches are paid. The division also matters a lot: FBS programs earn much more than similar programs in lower divisions.

This research has some limitations. The results only show relations, not causes. Since revenue has to cover the expenses of a program, variables such as coach salaries partly reflect the budget itself. The data are reported by the institutions themselves and describe only one point in time, and some missing salaries had to be filled in with the median. In addition, the components are formed without looking at revenue, so football, which is important for the largest programs, is not well captured by them. Finally, the models were compared on only one train/test split, so the small difference between them may change with another split. Future research could use data from several years, repeat the split several times, and add variables that are directly related to income, such as attendance or media contracts.
